# chirp

**Reads, edits and writes the memory channels of hundreds of radios**

- **Version recorded:** 20250530
- **Categories:** `radio-programming`, `rig-control`
- **Upstream:** <https://chirpmyradio.com/>
- **Supersedes:** `owx`

## What it does

Reads the memory image out of a handheld or mobile transceiver over its programming cable, presents the channels as a spreadsheet -- frequency, tone, offset, name, power -- lets you edit them, and writes the image back. It also imports from other radios, from CSV, and from online repeater directories.

## Why you would want it

Programming a modern handheld from its own keypad is genuinely awful, and the manufacturer software is Windows-only, per-model, and frequently worse. CHIRP does every common radio from one interface, and it lets you keep a channel list as a file that can be edited, versioned and copied to the next radio. For anyone with more than one radio it is not optional.

## Before it will work

The right programming cable, and access to its serial device -- the `dialout` group. Many cheap cables use counterfeit chips; see below.

## How it installs

- apt: `chirp`
  - AHRL installs a bundled wheel with `pipx install --system-site-packages` run as the user through pkexec, then generates a `run_chirp` wrapper because pipx installs into the user's home (inventory unit 84). Debian packages it, so this is apt -- and it is one of the few packages in this catalog where Parrot differs from Debian: Parrot carries a patched 1:20250530-1parrot1 against Debian 13's 1:20250502-1, with Ubuntu and Kali on 1:20251108-1 and Mint on 1:20240224-1 (measured 2026-08-28). CHIRP is versioned by release date, so those gaps are months of radio support.

## Known problems

Counterfeit Prolific and FTDI cables are the dominant problem in this whole area. A cable may enumerate, appear in `dmesg`, and still fail to communicate, because the driver detects the clone and refuses. Buy from a known source. Always download from the radio before uploading to it: the downloaded image is your only backup, and a wrong model selection can write an image the radio cannot boot from. Some radios are known to CHIRP only in a development build, which is why the version spread across targets matters.

## Keeping it current

- probe: apt policy
- strategy: apt_upgrade
- Upstream releases continuously and versions by date. New radio models appear in new builds and nowhere else, so a radio that is not in the list is often a matter of the version rather than of support.

## Where to get help with the software itself

The CHIRP project. Its own site carries per-model instructions, which are the answer to most "does it support my radio" questions.
